source: CARE Cambodia (Pailin), "TIP Training on Maize Production" / បទដ្ឋានអនុវត្ដបច្ចេកវិទ្យា ផលិតកម្មដំណំពូតក្របម, 2009. Funded by AusAID (ACIMA project), the European Union (Pailin Food Security Program), and ACIAR (CCPMP project). Nutrient section cites IPNI (International Plant Nutrition Institute) as a data source.
text:
Soil with good fertility plays a major role in achieving high crop yield. Corn requires a high amount of nitrogen to reach high yield. Although the atmosphere itself contains large quantities of nitrogen, corn cannot use atmospheric nitrogen gas directly; it can only take up nitrogen from the soil in dissolved/ionic forms. Nitrogen fertilizer is supplied from many different sources and chemical forms (examples listed in the source include ammonia, ammonium hydroxide, ammonium sulfate, urea, and sodium nitrate), and corn generally absorbs nitrogen from the soil in ammonium and nitrate forms.

Nitrogen applied to soil is mobile — it moves away from where it was originally placed — and is also easily lost from the soil through runoff, evaporation/volatilization, and leaching. Because of this high mobility and loss rate, nitrogen fertilizer should be split and applied across multiple growth stages rather than in a single application.

Symptoms of nitrogen deficiency: stunted growth with weak overall plant development; leaves develop a pale yellow-green striping, starting with the older, lower leaves, which die back first. Ears become smaller, grain protein content drops, and overall yield is reduced.
